summary:
Nothing in Honduran law criminalises gender identity. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Honduras since 1899, with the age of consent set at 15 years for both same-sex and heterosexual conduct.

The Penal Code, amended by Decree No. 23-2013 and in force since March 2017, treats hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating circumstance for criminal responsibility under Article 27. Article 321 punishes anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies individual or collective rights or refuses a professional service on those grounds with three to five years imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages. Article 321-A punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred, contempt, persecution, violence or attacks on those grounds with three to five years imprisonment and a fine of L.50,000 to L.300,000. The provisions were retained in the new Code after LGBTI rights groups met with Congress on the wording.

The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs permits arrest of anyone who goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals. LGBTI organizations have documented numerous instances in which police have used this provision as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space.

Human Rights Watch reported in May 2009 that police in Honduras subjected transgender people to rape, assault and extortion. International human rights organizations have stated that the military government targeted LGBTI people for harassment, abuse and murder.

Honduras holds transgender women in the men's penitentiary system, with no placement by gender identity policy. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the La Isla module beside the unit for mentally ill prisoners. Trans women there are forced to cut their hair, barred from presenting as women and denied conjugal visits. At Penitenciaria de Marcala, authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after intervention by the torture prevention centre CPTRT was she separated from men and her belongings returned.

Human Rights Watch confirmed in 2020 that Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which can lead to physical and sexual abuse. A Honduran judge described a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of guards. The judge had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate.

Same-sex unions are not legally recognized. A 2005 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage and de facto unions, refuses recognition of same-sex marriages or unions legally performed in other countries under Article 112, and prohibits adoption by same-sex couples under Article 116. Same-sex couples lack the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples.

Registered violence includes 69 transgender persons among 174 violent LGBTI deaths between 2009 and 2014, and 264 LGBTI people murdered between 2009 and 2017, concentrated in Cortes and Francisco Morazan. Transgender activist Cynthia Nicole was shot dead on 2 January, and trans activist Thalia Rodriguez was murdered on 10 January 2022 in Tegucigalpa. In June 2013 Spain granted asylum to a transsexual woman from Honduras after a police officer attempted to assassinate her. Vicky Hernandez v. Honduras, heard at the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case.

Impunity is structural. LGBTI persons, particularly trans women, face major obstacles to justice linked to under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources and intentional mishandling of cases. The United States Department of State 2021 Human Rights Report listed violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, corruption and lack of accountability for gender-based violence.

Official hostility is on record. President Juan Orlando Hernandez said on 12 October 2018 that as a Christian he was personally against same-sex marriage. The president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors Association urged President Xiomara Castro to stop immoral laws. The two major parties have largely ignored LGBTI rights.
tangentialFactors:
Honduran groups describe a social environment of historical discrimination against LGBTI persons motivated by prejudice and machismo. No sourced statement addresses societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.

Human Rights Watch finds that states in Central America exclude transgender women from femicide legal frameworks. Officials in Guatemala have described trans women as not biological women for this purpose.

Honduras and El Salvador are reported among the countries with the highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons. Coverage of Honduras between 2004 and 2011 records church protests against state recognition of gay groups in August 2004, murders of LGBTI activists amid impunity in 2009 and 2010, and post-coup abuses against gay communities.

About 400 people marched in a pride parade in July 2017 in San Pedro Sula. Three candidates who supported same-sex marriage before the November 2017 elections failed to win seats in the National Congress.
localsOnly:
Initial efforts to register an LGBTI rights group in the 1980s met government opposition or extended delay. Early organizations, often formed in response to the HIV/AIDS pandemic, held no legal standing and faced police harassment. In 2004 the government extended formal recognition to three LGBTI groups despite protests from the Catholic Church, Pentecostal churches and conservative legislators.

Trans people have sought electoral office. A co-founder of Asociacion Cozumel Trans ran for the Innovation and Unity Party in Francisco Morazan in the 26 November 2017 congressional election, in what was reported as a possible first openly trans officeholder. The record also notes Kendra Stefani Jordany's 2017 primary win, Claudia Spellman's 2012 run for LIBRE, and a transgender candidacy that received 11,112 votes and placed 136th for the 128-seat National Congress without success. Victoria Gomez sought asylum in Spain after threats and attacks in Tegucigalpa.

A name change for LGBTI persons is reported as approved, without procedure details. The president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors Association described it as an aberration in God's eyes.

After the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 on access to marriage, activists filed suit in the Supreme Court in May 2018 to legalise same-sex marriage. A second case was dismissed in November 2018 for technical errors. Deputy Manuel Rodriguez of Libertad y Refundacion presented a same-sex marriage bill to the National Congress in May 2022, under discussion since 24 May 2022.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry, visa, airport screening and document marker rules for trans visitors are not sourced in the inventory. No bathroom or facilities law specific to Honduras is sourced.

Access to gender-affirming care, including any ban, and youth-specific care provisions are not sourced. General references to government medical care and HIV awareness work do not establish trans-specific care rules.

The procedure, eligibility and evidentiary requirements for the reported approval of name changes for LGBTI persons are not sourced. The exact year of the killing of Cynthia Nicole is not sourced beyond the 2 January date given.
